overview:
Samuel grows old and makes his sons judges at Beer-sheba, but they take bribes and pervert judgment. The elders come to him at Ramah and ask, “make us a king to judge us like all the nations.” Displeased, Samuel prays. The LORD tells him to listen: the people have rejected the LORD, not Samuel, as they have since Egypt. Samuel must warn them what a king will do. He will take their sons, daughters, fields and servants and a tenth of their harvest and flocks, and they will cry out and not be heard. The people refuse: they want a king to judge them and fight their battles. The LORD says to give them one.

Three times the LORD tells Samuel, “Hearken unto their voice” (vv. 7, 9, 22). He grants the request he calls a rejection of himself, and sends it forward with a warning attached.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. The Talmud credits Samuel, with Gad and Nathan completing it (1 Chronicles 29:29); many scholars see it as part of a larger history compiled in the 7th–6th century BC from older sources.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it soon after the events (11th–10th century BC); many scholars date its final form to the 7th–6th century BC, drawing on older court and prophetic sources.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Late in Samuel’s life, just before Saul, in the later 11th century BC. Whiston’s margins to Josephus date the request for a king to 1116 BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Ramah, Samuel’s home town in mount Ephraim (1:1, 19); his sons sit as judges at Beer-sheba in the far south.

hermeneutics:
Samuel’s “manner of the king” (vv. 11–17) describes how kingship in Canaan actually worked. In 1956 Isaac Mendelsohn compared it with Akkadian texts from Ugarit and Alalakh in Syria (14th–13th century BC). There kings kept a class of chariot warriors in their service, drafted men for royal estates and workshops, and seized land and granted it to their officials. Samuel’s list follows the same order: sons for chariots and horsemen (v. 11), plowing, harvest and weapon-making (v. 12), and the best fields handed to the king’s servants (v. 14). The warning describes the known practice of the very nations Israel wanted to resemble.

The royal tithe was real as well. A tithe is attested at Ugarit in the 14th century BC, and one text there records the king granting the tithe of a whole town to an official for loyal service. Verse 15 says the same: the king will take a tenth of seed and vineyards “and give to his officers, and to his servants.” Israel’s law had already called the tithe the LORD’s (Leviticus 27:30). Here a king claims a tenth of seed and flock for himself (vv. 15, 17).

The Hebrew of v. 16 has the king take “your goodliest young men” between the servants and the asses. The Septuagint reads “your good herds,” which pairs men and women servants with cattle and asses, and the NRSV follows it. The two readings differ by a few letters in Hebrew.

structure.summary: An inclusio: the people’s demand for a king “like all the nations” opens and closes the exchange (vv. 5, 20).

open.text: Make us a king to judge us like all the nations

close.text: That we also may be like all the nations

rows.label: B
rows.text: The LORD: hearken unto their voice, and protest

notes: **Hearken:** *shama’* comes 5 times, four of them with “the voice”: the LORD’s “hearken unto the voice” (vv. 7, 9, 22) against the people who “refused to obey the voice of Samuel” (v. 19).
**Take:** the verb *laqach* comes 4 times in the warning (vv. 11, 13, 14, 16), with “take the tenth” twice more (vv. 15, 17). It began with the sons who “took bribes” (v. 3).
**Servants:** the king’s servants get your fields and tithes (vv. 14, 15), your own servants are taken (v. 16), and the list ends, “ye shall be his servants” (v. 17).

Chapter 8 opens the second part of the book, “A king like the nations: Saul” (8:1–15:35). The judges’ order fails the way Eli’s house did, through sons unfit to succeed their father (2:12; 8:3). The chapter ends with no king named; the next scene starts with a Benjamite looking for his father’s asses (9:1–3).

**Backward and forward:** Deuteronomy 17:14 foresees Israel saying, “I will set a king over me, like as all the nations.” Gideon had refused the crown because “the LORD shall rule over you” (Judges 8:23), and Samuel returns to the request in his farewell (12:12, 19).

traditions.text: A thematic parallel. When the Jaredites ask their leaders to anoint one of their sons king, the request grieves them, and the brother of Jared warns, “Surely this thing leadeth into captivity.” Two generations later Corihor rebels against his father, King Kib, gathers an army and takes him captive, and Ether notes that this brought to pass the brother of Jared’s saying. Samuel’s warning runs the same direction, ending with the people as the king’s servants (v. 17), and both records follow the request to the loss of freedom it was warned to bring.

The Church’s footnote to v. 7, “Hearken unto the voice of the people,” points to King Mosiah’s law for the Nephites. He tells them it is not common for the voice of the people to desire what is wrong, so they should do their business by that voice. But if the time comes that the voice of the people chooses iniquity, then the judgments of God will come. Israel’s voice in 1 Samuel 8 is heard and granted, with that kind of warning attached.

The footnote to v. 18, “the LORD will not hear you in that day,” points to Limhi’s people in bondage to the Lamanites. There the Lord was slow to hear their cry because of their iniquities, yet he did hear: he softened their captors’ hearts and eased their burdens, though he did not yet free them. The Book of Mormon account shows what Samuel’s warning can look like when a people cries out under a yoke of its own making.

The midrash reads the warning of v. 18 forward into Israel’s history. When kings arose over Israel and began to oppress them, it says, God answered their complaint: did you not forsake me and ask for a king yourselves? It pairs this with the psalm’s counsel, “Put not your trust in princes” (Psalm 146:3), and praises the one who trusts in God instead.

Josephus places Samuel’s sons at Bethel and Beer-sheba, where v. 2 has both at Beer-sheba, and says they turned to luxury and costly living. He explains Samuel’s displeasure by his politics: Samuel hated kingly government and was very fond of aristocracy. The request so troubled him that he could neither eat nor sleep and lay awake all night.

In his retelling of vv. 11–17 the king uses Israel’s sons “as if they were slaves bought with money.” Daughters will do the work of women slaves who fear the whip, and the people’s land goes to the king’s eunuchs and bodyguards. The people answer that it is no absurdity to have the same government as their neighbors.

Here the people cite Moses, that they must surely appoint a prince over them (Deuteronomy 17), and Samuel grieves because they ask “a king before the time.” He fears this means no lasting kingdom yet and no house of the Lord. God answers that he will send them a king who will lay them waste and then be laid waste himself.

The rabbis read this chapter through the law of the king in Deuteronomy 17:14. Rabbi Nehorai calls the request an insult to Israel, citing v. 7, and says they wanted a king only to take up foreign worship, citing “that we also may be like all the nations” (v. 20). Rabbi Judah objects that the Torah commands a king; Israel was punished in Samuel’s day only because they took the initiative and asked too soon.

Was the manner of the king a grant of royal rights or only a warning? Shmuel and Rabbi Yosei say a king may do everything in vv. 11–17. Rav and Rabbi Yehuda say the passage was spoken only to make the people stand in awe of the king. Rabbi Nehorai holds that the whole request was a complaint, and Rabbi Eliezer splits the blame: the elders asked properly for a king “to judge us,” but the ignorant ruined it by adding “like all the nations” (vv. 19–20).

Rashi locates Samuel’s displeasure in the words “to judge us,” as the nations’ kings judge. Commentators on Rashi explain that Deuteronomy 17 permits a king, so the fault was not in asking for one but in the motive, rejecting Samuel to be like the nations. The reading agrees with Rabbi Eliezer in the Talmud.
